Where it began

Richard Hadlee was born in Christchurch on 3 July 1951, into a family that had cricket running through it. His father, Walter Hadlee, played for New Zealand, and so did two of Richard's four brothers, Dayle and Barry. He was born in the St Albans part of the city and went to Fendalton Open Air School.

He first played for Canterbury in 1971/72 and reached Test cricket in 1973. On both debuts his very first ball went for four, which is the kind of start that teaches a young bowler patience.

The player

Over 86 Tests between 1973 and 1990 he took 431 wickets at 22.30, with 36 five-wicket innings and nine ten-wicket matches. He also made 3,124 runs at 27.17, with two hundreds and 15 fifties, the higher of them an unbeaten 151 in Sri Lanka.

The big days came in a steady line. He took 11 wickets against India in 1976 to win a Test, and six for 26 in 1978 as New Zealand beat England for the first time. At Brisbane in 1985 he took nine for 52 and then six more, and New Zealand went on to win a series in Australia for the first time. In 1988, in Bangalore, he became the leading wicket-taker in Test history, and in February 1990, in front of his home crowd at Christchurch, he became the first bowler to reach 400.

What made him special

He began as a very fast young bowler and became something better: a precise one. He cut down his run, kept a tight line close to the stumps and moved the ball both ways, with the outswinger as his favourite weapon. Batsmen found he rarely gave them anything to hit, and many were trapped in front.

At Nottinghamshire he was close to unplayable, and in 1984 he did the rare county double of 1,000 runs and 100 wickets. With the bat he was a hard-hitting left-hander, happier against lesser attacks than the very best, which seems a fair arrangement for a man who had usually just bowled the other side out.

Away from the middle

He was made an MBE in 1980 and was knighted in 1990, before he had played his last Test. He liked to point out that knighted cricketers were mostly batsmen, so he could claim to be the first bowler honoured since Sir Francis Drake. He marked the news by making 86 in the next Test.

Later he chaired New Zealand's selectors and set up a trust to help young Canterbury sportspeople facing hardship. In 2009 the ICC added him to its Hall of Fame, and a bronze bust of him stands in Christchurch.

And finally

When Wisden asked Walter Hadlee to name his five cricketers of the century, he put his own son on the list and admitted to some embarrassment in doing so. He had weighed Dennis Lillee too, but the numbers settled it. Even a proud father, it seems, could not argue with Richard's figures, and with the last ball of his Test career he took a wicket.
